## Film Photography Renaissance: Velvia 50 and the Mamiya 6

The /fgt/ (Film General Thread) on 4chan continues to be a vibrant hub for analog enthusiasts, blending technical gear discussions with personal shooting habits. A standout update involves a user’s bulk purchase of 18–20 rolls of Fujifilm Velvia 50 slide film. Despite expecting edge fogging on two open packages, the resulting slides were described as visually excellent, validating the film’s high color rendition and sharpness even with minor physical storage imperfections. This positive review serves as a practical endorsement for photographers considering bulk buys of open-stock slide film.

Conversely, not all gear news is glowing. User @4529593 posted a negative review of the Mamiya 6 rangefinder, labeling it a "FAIL." This critique adds to the ongoing community debate regarding the reliability of classic medium-format equipment, suggesting that even beloved cameras have their pitfalls. The thread also remains anchored by the recurring question of whether participants shoot film after switching from digital or have maintained an analog workflow since the beginning, with one user confirming they actively shoot both formats.

## Gear Wars: Canon vs. Fujifilm and Build Quality

A new motto has emerged in the /gear/ section: "gear only matters if your photo doesn't suck." This sentiment sparked a playful rivalry between camera brands, specifically targeting the "tryhard" tendencies of Fujifilm users who have switched to Canon. One commenter mocked @cANON for utilizing specific accessories like gaffer tape and Peak Design quick-release anchors, arguing that this heavy reliance on specialized gear is a hallmark of insecure "Fujislug" enthusiasts trying to compensate for skill deficits.

The discussion delved into a critical analysis of build quality, with users scrutinizing minor physical imperfections on a recent camera body. Complaints focused on a remaining port cover and rip rubber corners that were failing to stay attached. This granular focus on wear and tear suggests that the community’s tolerance for hardware flaws is low, implying that even minor durability issues can significantly impact the perceived value of expensive equipment.

## Retro Computing: Rust Emulator 'Snow' Joins Infinite Mac

In a significant update for retro computing enthusiasts, @Third Foundation announced the integration of "Snow," a Rust-based emulator, into the "Infinite Mac" project. The goal is to eventually replace the long-standing Mini vMac emulator. The author highlights Snow’s active community, well-structured codebase, and, crucially, higher accuracy in replicating early Mac hardware limitations.

A key differentiator cited is Snow’s strict adherence to the fact that the original Mac 128K lacked first-party hard drives. Unlike Mini vMac, which allowed users to "cheat" by patching the ROM to simulate an "Infinite HD" with 1.4 MB of software—an anachronism—Snow does not support this. While the integration required adding a layer of indirection for file I/O and audio, the maintainer was open to merging these Infinite Mac-specific changes, signaling a promising future for accurate, legacy-first emulation.

## Tech Frustrations and Fast Food Analogies

Not all social media activity is technical. On Bluesky, user @Sham Iamb contributed a terse, universal expression of tech discontent: "Man fuck computer." This cryptic post reflects the ubiquitous sentiment of annoyance directed at digital devices, likely triggered by a recent glitch or poor user experience. It serves as a reminder that despite our love for gadgets, frustration remains a constant companion.

In the realm of consumer culture, @lilylasthope offered a humorous comparison between fast-food giants. Asserting that widely accepted opinions regarding Popeyes biscuits accurately describe Bojangles chicken, the post leverages a popular internet meme format. It implies that Bojangles’ chicken possesses the same beloved, biscuit-like characteristics or overall comfort-food appeal as the viral Popeyes biscuits, elevating the latter to the same status in the minds of followers.

## Ken Rockwell’s "Crazy" Colors

Photography critic Ken Rockwell remains a focal point of discussion, particularly regarding his aesthetic preferences. A photo of Rockwell wearing a blue shirt patterned with classic sports cars was highlighted as evidence of his fondness for "crazy" colors. Participants cited his Leica Q3 review and a YouTube clip where he explicitly states he "likes things crazy" regarding color choices. The consensus is that Rockwell’s distinct visual style—featuring bold, exaggerated palettes—is a deliberate artistic choice rather than an accident.

## Quick Hits

*   **Olympus D545 Zoom Quirks:** Users on Newsblur are discussing specific malfunctions with the vintage Olympus d545 zoom camera. The thread invites other owners to confirm if reported issues are common defects for this discontinued model, reflecting a broader trend of troubleshooting older digital photography equipment.
*   **Final Fantasy VII Remake Inquiry:** A single post on Newsblur under the #ff7 tag solicits community opinions on the narrative and gameplay alterations in the *Final Fantasy VII Remake* trilogy. The open-ended inquiry invites players to compare the remake’s evolving storyline and design choices against the classic original.

representative_texts: @Third Foundation (rayckeith@techhub.social) — "It was thus fortuitous that Snow was released late last year. It’s an emulator that covers the same era1 as Mini vMac, with a focus on accuracy. It also happens to be written in Rust, and has an active maintainer and community. I set out to bring up Snow as a new emulator core inside Infinite Mac, with the goal of eventually replacing my use of Mini vMac. Snow is a well-structured codebase; there’s already a separation between the core and the native frontend. It was pretty natural to add a new crate that hooked up the core to the Infinite Mac abstractions for video, input, audio, disk images, etc. For file I/O and audio, Snow didn’t quite have the flexibility I needed, but it was feasible to add a layer of indirection. The maintainer was open to merging these changes; my fork is mostly Infinite Mac-specific work, and thus easy to keep up to date. The flipside of Snow being a more accurate emulator is that it also replicates the limitations of early Mac hardware. For example, the original Mac 128K only had an internal 400K floppy drive, and a connector for attaching an external one. But there was no first-party hard drive (at least, not without hacks) and third-party ones sound finicky2. Mini vMac did not quite operate at that level (it instead patches the ROM and relies on that custom driver) and thus it was possible to “cheat” – I had simulated an “Infinite HD” for it with 1.4 MB of installed software, even though that was anachronistic3." # retroComputing  # mac https:// blog.persistent.info/2026/09/i nfinite-mac-snow-and-aux.html

A key distinction cited is Snow’s higher accuracy in replicating early Mac hardware limitations, such as the lack of first-party hard drives in the original Mac 128K. This contrasts with Mini vMac, which previously allowed "cheating" by patching the ROM to simulate an "Infinite HD" with 1.4 MB of software, an anachronism Snow does not support.
